summary: This RFC describes requirements for a graphical format for an online graphical communication protocol and proposes an Interactive Graphical Communication Format based on the GKSM session metafile. The authors hoped it would spark discussion of multimedia data exchange.

eli5.summary: A plan to let people send drawings to each other over the network, with a shared way of describing the picture.

questions: how to send graphics over a network
how to exchange drawings between computers
subtitle: A format for exchanging interactive graphics commands between networked workstations.

tldr.problem: Computers with graphics displays need a standard way to send and receive drawing commands and graphical objects over the network. Without a common format, different graphics systems cannot share pictures or work together in real-time graphical sessions like conferencing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes the Interactive Graphical Communication Format (IGCF), based on the GKSM session metafile standard. It adds elements for object definition, instantiation, and manipulation on top of the GKSM graphics primitives, allowing systems to exchange both drawing commands and semantic objects while transmitting efficiently over narrow-bandwidth channels.
tldr.outcome: The proposal provides a blueprint for multimedia conferencing systems and interactive graphics applications that need to work together. It builds on an existing standard (GKSM) to ensure compatibility with the large GKS user base.

today: RFC 965 proposes a vector graphics protocol format for interactive workstations. While GKS and GKSM were significant standards in the 1980s, the graphics landscape evolved significantly. However, the RFC's concepts influenced later graphics communication standards and remains relevant for understanding how to structure interchange formats for interactive graphics.

sections.title: The Need for a Graphics Protocol
sections.content:
In the mid-1980s, computers with high-resolution graphics displays were becoming more common. A graphical communication protocol is needed so that two or more workstations can exchange interactive vector graphics, possibly along with voice or video in a multimedia conference.

Vector graphics (commands like draw a line, fill a polygon) are far more compact than sending bitmapped images, because the receiving computer can redraw locally. This lets graphical workstations exchange drawing commands and share a workspace in real time, much like an audio-graphics conference where participants see and manipulate the same drawing.

Existing graphics standards like NAPLPS (for videotex) and the Computer Graphics Interface focus on one-way transmission or device control rather than peer-to-peer interactive exchange. The RFC argues for a new format specifically designed for online interaction among intelligent workstations.
sections.eli5: When two people have computers with drawing programs and want to work on the same picture together over the network, they need a way to understand each other. The RFC looks for that way.

sections.title: Operational Requirements for IGCF
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven key requirements for an IGCF:

Interoperation of heterogeneous systems: The format must let different graphics packages and hardware platforms work together, like connecting a CAD editor to a graphical database.

Picture capture: The format must handle both static pictures (final results) and dynamic exchanges during interactive sessions, and support graphical libraries with reusable objects.

Prompt transmission: For real-time conferencing, construction and manipulation must be transmitted as they happen, but only at useful granularity (completed objects, not partial strokes).

Low traffic volume: The format should minimize network bandwidth by reusing objects and including basic primitives from which complex shapes are built.

Preservation of application semantics: Objects like navy carriers or CAD parts are treated as units with identity, not as collections of individual graphics elements, reducing both traffic and processing.

Transmission batching: Updates that change the picture are sent immediately; updates to internal data structures can be batched until a visible change occurs.

Simple translation: There must be a straightforward mapping between user interface commands and IGCF elements.
sections.eli5: The format needs to: work on different computers, let people share libraries, go fast for live collaboration, not use too much bandwidth, treat objects as whole units, batch less important updates, and be easy to translate.

sections.title: Elements and Architecture of IGCF
sections.content:
IGCF is structured in two layers. Level L is the GKSM (Graphical Kernel System Metafile) specification, which defines the graphics primitives and attributes. Level U adds new elements for interactive graphical applications: object definition and manipulation, segment transformations, visibility control, pointer tracking, and rubber-band feedback.

Object hierarchies allow complex objects to be built from simpler ones. Each object has an identifier that is independent of the communication session and the local system, so objects defined in one session can be reused in others. Operations on objects include transformation (rotation, scaling), deletion, display, hide, expose (bring to front), and component selection.

For coordinates, the format uses normalized device coordinates (NDC) for network transmission, with the option to map between world coordinates and NDC at each workstation. This lets each system display the shared workspace in the most convenient portion of its screen.
sections.eli5: The format has two levels: a basic level for drawing (lines, polygons, text) and an advanced level for treating named objects as units, transforming them, and showing or hiding them. Objects can be made from other objects, like Lego blocks.

sections.title: IGCF Elements and Message Format
sections.content:
The RFC details the IGCF elements and their encoding. Level U elements are encoded as GKSM user items so a PIGCF (proposed IGCF) file is a complete GKSM metafile.

Object definition: BEGIN DEFINITION and END DEFINITION mark a sequence of graphics commands that define a reusable object with an identifier.

Object instantiation: BEGIN INSTANTIATION and END INSTANTIATION place a previously defined object into the current picture with specified transformation parameters.

Object manipulation: Commands like TRANSFORM OBJECT, DELETE OBJECT, DISPLAY OBJECT, DISAPPEAR OBJECT, EXPOSE OBJECT, and HIDE OBJECT operate on named objects.

Dynamics: POINTER TRACKING transmits sampled points from a graphical pointer trace. RUBBER BAND shows dynamic feedback (line, rectangle, or circle) as the user moves the pointer.

Coordinate transformation: SET WINDOW and SET VIEWPORT define the mapping between world coordinates and the NDC display area.
sections.eli5: The messages say things like 'start defining an object', 'place this object here', 'move that object', 'the pointer is at this location', and 'draw a feedback line from here to there'.

sections.title: Software Architecture for IGCF Processing
sections.content:
The RFC describes how IGCF fits into a graphics conferencing system. The application generates level U elements (object operations); the graphics package generates level L elements (GKSM primitives). A router merges both streams and sends them to transmission, recording, and reception modules.

The transmission module batches level U updates until a level L update occurs, timestamps the stream for synchronization with other media, and sends it to remote stations. Different traffic categories (pointer updates, object definitions, library transfers) can use different transport services (real-time, reliable, best-effort).

The receive module unmarshals incoming streams, merges multiple traffic categories, checks timestamps, and validates syntax and semantics. Level L items go to the GKSM interpreter; level U items update the application's object structures. A recorder saves the full stream for later playback.
sections.eli5: A graphics conferencing system has modules that generate IGCF messages from user actions, transmit and receive them over the network, record them, and interpret them to update the display.
